name: Setting spray

lead: Setting spray is a liquid applied as a mist after makeup. Its purpose is to help the base look last, reducing creasing, fading and transfer, so skin looks even for more hours. Some versions aim for a matte finish and others for a dewy one.
It sits in the same role as setting powder, which has long been used to lock in foundation and concealer and limit creasing and cracks.

paras: It is used as the last step after foundation, concealer, powder and blush, sprayed over the face from a short distance and left to dry. Makeup artists and creators pair it with primers and powders as part of a long-wear routine; some use it before powder to melt layers together.

Ingredients vary by product. Alcohol-based sprays can feel drying, and fragrance or preservatives may irritate sensitive skin or cause allergic reactions. Product labels advise keeping the mist away from the eyes.

angle.text: Setting spray helps makeup look the same later in the day as when it was applied, which keeps the skin tone and finish even for longer.

lead: Setting spray is a cosmetic mist applied over finished makeup to help it stay in place. People use it to keep foundation and concealer from creasing or fading, so their complexion looks consistent through the day or an event.

It works alongside setting powder, which is an older technique. Face powder has been described as a staple for setting makeup in place since the 1990s, and translucent powder in the "baking" method is said to give long wear.[1] Sprays are an alternative or addition, formulated to leave a thin film over the makeup.
No published clinical studies were found testing setting sprays, and this article relies on how cosmetics sources describe the category.

paras: Setting sprays come in matte, dewy and "natural" finishes and are marketed as long-wear or fixing sprays. They are used with powder, primer and foundation as one set of steps.

Loose powder sets foundation and concealer, smoothing the complexion and limiting cracks and lines, and pressed powder can do the same. Translucent powder in baking is described as giving long-lasting wear.[1]
Reports of reactions concern fragrance and alcohol in some formulas; label guidance advises avoiding the eyes.
